solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Service providers in Scottish town protected by those in charge

indicators.note: the town is sheltered inside the other word, which wraps round it

parts.note: the people in charge; this word wraps round the town, after its first letter
Ayr, a town on the Scottish west coast

explanation.surface: A Scottish town's services are run under the eye of the local bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service providers' sounds like utilities, but the services are church services: lay readers are non-clergy who lead them.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay readers are laypeople licensed to conduct church services, so they literally provide services.

clue.text: I distract elk roaming in national park

indicators.note: the letters wander about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of drawing the attention of an elk wandering through a national park.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lake District is a national park in Cumbria, north-west England, famous for its lakes and fells.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this Cumbrian region is one of the national parks of England and Wales.

clue.text: I agree to eat a starter of toasted fungus

parts.note: 'yes' is what you say when you agree

indicators.note: the starter is the first letter

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic diner agrees to try a toasted mushroom starter.
explanation.walkthrough: The meal picture hides a baker's ingredient: yeast is a single-celled fungus.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeast is a microscopic fungus used in baking and brewing.

clue.text: Before and after evening drinks

indicators.note: the phrase swallows the answer, holding it inside

parts.note: the last two letters of 'after' plus the first of 'evening'

explanation.surface: A note of drinks served before and after an evening meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before and after' reads as a pair of times, but only 'Before' is the definition; 'after' starts the phrase that holds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though an old-fashioned, poetic one, as in 'ere long'.

clue.text: Calling briefly for leather protector

indicators.note: cut short: the last letter is dropped

parts.note: DUBBING (calling, naming) without its final G

explanation.surface: Someone phones up quickly to order some leather polish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling' looks like a phone call; here it is naming, as in to dub someone a knight. Dubbin is a grease used to waterproof leather boots.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubbin is a wax-and-oil dressing rubbed into leather to soften and waterproof it.

clue.text: Helen rips pants and top up

indicators.note: British slang for rubbish: the letters are a mess

explanation.surface: Helen tears her trousers and her shirt in a wardrobe mishap.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants and top look like clothes; 'pants' is the British slang for rubbish, and 'top up' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To replenish something is to fill it up again, or top it up.

clue.text: Bad behaviour when driving to Leeds, perhaps, is illusion

parts.note: the M1 motorway runs from London to Leeds; the 1 is written as I
road rage, the bad temper of drivers

explanation.surface: Road rage on the way to Leeds turns out to be a trick of the mind.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the main motorway from London to Leeds; crosswords read the digit 1 as the letter I. Blocks run in answer order, so M1 comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion, such as water seen on a hot road.

clue.text: A politician affected by temperature on stage

parts.note: hit = affected, as in 'hit by the cuts'

explanation.surface: An MP on a platform is sweating under the hot lights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' reads as a platform for the politician, but it is the definition: an amphitheatre is an arena for performance.
explanation.definitionFit: An amphitheatre is an open-air arena or stage where performances are held.

clue.text: Jack delivered part of church

indicators.note: a speech is delivered, so the words are spoken

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church; add a silent K and the sound is unchanged

explanation.surface: A man called Jack brought round a section of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: In playing cards the jack is also called the knave.
explanation.definitionFit: Knave is the older name for the jack in a pack of cards.

clue.text: Bishop is primarily made to take appropriate sacrament

indicators.note: first and foremost: just the first letter

parts.note: apt = appropriate; taken in after B

explanation.surface: A bishop is obliged to receive the right sacrament.
explanation.walkthrough: Bishop, sacrament: the church setting is real, and the answer fits it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the rite of christening is one of the Christian sacraments.

clue.text: Resolve to put off excavation

explanation.surface: Someone decides to postpone digging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put off' reads as postpone, but the wordplay wants its other sense, discourage.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to resolve on something is to decide it firmly.

clue.text: Gang fight with a sword put to one side

parts.note: a ring is a gang, as in a smuggling ring

explanation.surface: A street gang settles a quarrel with a sword before putting it away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put to one side' seems to be the sword being laid down; it is the definition, as money is ring-fenced for one purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring-fence funds is to set them aside so they can be used only for one purpose.

clue.text: Tree has changed

indicators.note: the letters are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A tree has altered, perhaps with the seasons.
explanation.walkthrough: A three-letter anagram is short enough to try every order; the definition sits first.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a common European tree with winged seeds.

clue.text: Hairdresser's in small town on a regular basis

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals: every other one

parts.note: S m A l L t O w N: the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th letters

explanation.surface: A hairdresser's in a little town that people visit regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairdresser's' is short for hairdresser's shop, so it matches a salon; 'on' belongs to the indicator, not the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive stands for the shop, as in 'going to the hairdresser's', which is the premises where hair is styled.

clue.text: Spread foam over someone using metalworking tool?

definitions.meaning: to cover with soapy froth, as a barber does before a shave
the tool is a lathe; add -ER for the person working it, as baker from bake

explanation.surface: A barber soaps a customer's face, or a workshop hand at the lathe.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is invented: LATHE plus -ER, like a baker or a miner, and the question mark owns up to it.
explanation.definitionFit: To lather is to spread foam; a 'lather' is jokingly one who uses a lathe.

clue.text: Starting late, winter is unsettled still

indicators.note: the word begins a letter late, losing its first letter
the letters are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: The weather report: winter has come late and is still changeable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' at the end looks like an adverb, 'is still unsettled'; it is the definition, meaning motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: Inert means still, without motion.

clue.text: Harry, after taking coat, is in French nick

indicators.note: once its coat is taken off, the word loses its outer letters
translate the word into French

parts.note: HARRY without its outer letters H and Y

explanation.surface: Prince Harry, having taken someone's coat, ends up in a French police cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' is British slang for arrest (and also for a police station, which the surface leans on).
explanation.definitionFit: To nick someone is British slang for to arrest them.

clue.text: Part of brutal routine

indicators.note: the answer is a piece of the next word

parts.note: the second, third and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A grim description of a harsh daily grind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of brutal routine' reads as one phrase; 'Part of' governs only 'brutal', and 'routine' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: being stuck in a groove worn by wheels stands for a dull, unchanging routine.

clue.text: Grange Hill's opening bores distant timid individual

indicators.note: the opening is the first letter

parts.note: a timid person is a mouse
first letter of Hill, bored into MOUSE: M(H)OUSE

explanation.surface: The opening episode of Grange Hill bores a shy, far-off viewer.
explanation.walkthrough: Grange Hill was a long-running British children's TV drama set in a school; split off 'Grange' and it is a country house with farm buildings.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, chiefly British: a country house with farm buildings attached.

clue.text: Civic headwear scratches head

indicators.note: the head, the first letter, is scratched out

explanation.surface: A mayor's ceremonial hat makes its wearer's head itch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Civic headwear' reads as one phrase, a mayor's hat; the definition is 'Civic' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Civic and urban both mean belonging to a city or town.

clue.text: Disinfect lists in church

indicators.note: one word goes inside the other

parts.note: a ship lists when it tilts to one side; this sits between C and E

explanation.surface: Instructions to sanitise the lists posted up in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lists' looks like a noun for rosters; here it is a verb, leans to one side.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to rid something of dirt or germs.

clue.text: Taxi returned to Italian explorer

indicators.note: sent back, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: as written, then turned round to OT

explanation.surface: A taxi drops a passenger back at the house of an Italian explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: John Cabot was a Venetian navigator who sailed for England and reached North America in 1497.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cabot (Giovanni Caboto) was an Italian explorer.

clue.text: Company left in depression

explanation.surface: A firm is left in a slump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' suggests an economic slump for the company; it is a dip in a mountain ridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A col is a low point, or depression, in a ridge between two peaks.

clue.text: Plague pees client off

indicators.note: gone off, spoiled: the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A pest annoys a customer until they leave in disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plague' reads as a verb, to pester; the answer is the noun, a deadly epidemic.
explanation.definitionFit: Pestilence is a deadly epidemic disease, a plague.
